docs.title: 8. Research Roadmap and Open Gaps
docs.text: A core failure mode of newly proposed indices is rushing to public scoring, commercial deployment, or national ranking before establishing basic psychometric validity. To prevent premature reification, this roadmap defines an 11-phase sequential research program with explicit, falsifiable gating criteria.

docs.title: 8.1 The 11-Phase Research Roadmap
docs.text:
Each phase requires satisfying pre-registered empirical criteria before the program is permitted to advance to subsequent phases:

Phase Phase Name & Operational Focus Key Technical Output Falsifiable Gating Criterion Phase 0 Conceptual Feasibility Audit (Current Report) Definitional boundaries, construct audit, and governance architecture. Formal go/no-go decision by sponsoring consortium. Phase 1 Systematic Literature Review Formal PRISMA-compliant systematic review of automation bias, reliance calibration, and AI literacy. Comprehensive evidence matrix published with zero unverified citations. Phase 2 Expert Delphi Study 2–3 rounds of structured feedback from 20–30 experts across cognitive psychology, HCI, AI alignment, psychometrics, and ethics. $\ge 70\%$ panel consensus on retained vs. pruned dimensions. Phase 3 Construct Operationalization Drafting item pools, task specifications, and stimulus matrices for retained dimensions. Content Validity Index ($S\text{-}CVI \ge 0.80$) approved by independent psychometrics panel. Phase 4 Exploratory Pilot Testing Small-scale administration ($n \approx 300$) of preliminary questionnaire batteries and baseline tasks. Internal consistency reliability ($\alpha \ge 0.70$, $\omega \ge 0.70$) across all subscales. Phase 5 Behavioral Experiment Calibration Implementation and calibration of the nine standardized behavioral AI experiments (Section 5). Experimental tasks demonstrate adequate item discrimination ($D \ge 0.30$) and test-retest stability ($r \ge 0.70$). Phase 6 Psychometric Validation (Decisive Phase) Pre-registered, large-scale empirical study testing construct, convergent, discriminant, and incremental validity. Demonstrated incremental validity: HSRI explains significant variance in override accuracy beyond existing standalone instruments ($\Delta R^2 > 0$). Phase 7 Cross-Cultural Invariance Testing Administration across at least three culturally distinct linguistic cohorts (MGCFA testing). Achievement of metric and scalar invariance across surveyed cohorts; non-invariant subscales quarantined. Phase 8 Prospective Longitudinal Studies 12-month follow-up tracking real-world professional and technical decision outcomes under AI assistance. Baseline HSRI profile prospectively predicts real-world error interception and preserved agency. Phase 9 Governed Individual / Org Release Deployment of diagnostic audit tools with active ethical governance and non-discrimination charters. Independent ethical governance board operational; commercial employment-screening bans enforced. Phase 10 National Composite Benchmarking Aggregation of independent national-level institutional, educational, and governance indicators. Independent econometric audit; strictly contingent on successful completion of Phases 1–8.

docs.title: 8.2 Critical Gating Rules
docs.text:
To protect scientific integrity, two inviolable gating rules govern this roadmap:

Rule 1: No Scale Development Prior to Delphi Consensus (Phases 1–2). Construct development and questionnaire creation (Phase 3) must not proceed until the PRISMA systematic review (Phase 1) is published and the expert Delphi consensus threshold ($\ge 70\%$) is reached.

Rule 2: Absolute Prohibition on Premature National Benchmarking. National-level composite scoring (Phase 10) must never be attempted based on aggregated individual survey data. National benchmarking may only evaluate structural institutional indicators (curricula, regulatory oversight, institutional trust) and is strictly conditioned on prior empirical validation of the individual construct (Phases 1–8).

docs.title: 8.3 Top Ten Open Research Gaps
docs.text:
The following ten empirical gaps must be resolved by the research community before HSRI can transition from a proposed construct to a validated instrument:

  1. Absence of an Integrated Empirical Battery: No validated instrument currently measures attentional control, metacognitive calibration, and automation-bias resistance jointly in an interactive AI environment.
  2. Generative-AI Deskilling Longitudinal Data: The literature lacks high-quality, pre-registered longitudinal evidence demonstrating permanent cognitive deskilling from long-term generative AI usage.
  3. Cross-Cultural Invariance in Human-AI Interaction: Zero studies have tested measurement invariance for decisional agency, automation bias, or calibrated trust across non-Western cultural samples.
  4. Prospective Predictive Validity: No empirical data currently connects laboratory performance on AI discernment tasks to real-world professional outcomes (e.g., medical error rates, legal drafting defects).
  5. Causal Direction of Value Clarity: The hypothesis that AI means-optimization increases the necessity of human ends-clarity remains a philosophical proposition lacking experimental verification [UNVERIFIED — NEEDS SOURCE].
  6. Task Isolation for Confident-Wrong AI Detection: Existing critical-thinking batteries fail to isolate the specific cognitive mechanisms involved in detecting fluent, authoritative machine hallucinations as distinct from general reasoning ability.
  7. Efficacy of Interventions: Evidence-based training interventions designed specifically to calibrate trust and reduce automation complacency under generative AI remain undeveloped.
  8. Mathematical Formulation of Critical-Weakness Floors: Empirical methodologies for establishing non-compensatory psychometric cutoffs in cognitive multi-task batteries lack standardized statistical precedents.
  9. Empirically Derived Weighting Functions: The optimal weighting scheme linking foundational substrates (Tier 1) and mediators (Tier 2) to interaction outcomes (Tier 3) cannot be specified prior to Phase 6 validation.
  10. Governance Frameworks for Psychological Benchmarks: Regulatory and ethical governance mechanisms for large-scale psychological indexing significantly lag behind those established for international economic indices.

docs.title: 9. Final Recommendation and Next Experiment
docs.text: This section synthesizes the feasibility review into a definitive operational verdict, selects the optimal structural model archetype, and defines the precise next empirical experiment required to test the construct.

docs.title: 9.1 Definitive Recommendation: Develop as a Research Construct First
docs.text:
The evaluation of conceptual foundations, psychometric redundancy, measurement architecture, and ethical risks leads to a single, unequivocal conclusion:

RECOMMENDATION: DEVELOP AS A RESEARCH CONSTRUCT FIRST.

This recommendation explicitly rejects three alternative courses of action:

  1. Rejection of "Develop a Public Index Now": Launching a public ranking, national leaderboard, or commercial workforce index today is scientifically indefensible. Zero validation data exists, psychometric properties are uncalibrated, and ethical safeguards against employment discrimination and responsibility laundering are unbuilt.
  2. Rejection of "Reject Concept as Wholly Redundant": While all underlying cognitive substrates have validated homes in established psychological literature, existing instruments study these capacities in isolation and outside the interactive context of capable AI systems. A narrow, defensible integration gap exists once the construct is operationalized around behavioral interaction under task asymmetry.
  3. Rejection of Passive "Wait for More Evidence": Resolving construct feasibility cannot be achieved through passive literature monitoring alone. Active, pre-registered empirical experiments are required to determine whether an integrated construct provides incremental predictive validity over separate instruments.

docs.title: 9.2 Structural Model Archetype Selection
docs.text:
Three candidate model archetypes were evaluated:

Model Archetype Structural Composition Methodological Advantages Fatal Flaws & Vulnerabilities Final Disposition Archetype 1: Conservative Model Strictly incorporates already-proven psychological instruments (ANT, IUS, Big Five). High initial psychometric validity; zero unverified constructs. Fatal redundancy: Merely re-badges existing cognitive psychology; fails to capture interactive human-AI dynamics. Rejected Archetype 2: Integrated Model (Recommended) Anchors foundational substrates (Tier 1–2) in validated instruments while focusing novel measurement on interactive behavioral tasks (Tier 3–4). Isolates the genuine research gap; directly tests behavioral override and calibrated trust under real AI asymmetry; avoids speculative futurology. Requires building and validating new interactive behavioral software environments. Selected & Recommended Archetype 3: Future-Oriented Model Introduces speculative constructs designed for hypothetical superintelligence (e.g., recursive self-improvement readiness, cosmic meaning preservation). Broad philosophical scope. High pseudoscience risk: Untestable against observable reality; ungrounded in empirical cognitive science. Rejected

docs.title: 9.3 Definitive Architectural Summary
docs.text:
• Operational Definition: The demonstrated behavioral capacity of an individual, organization, or society to maintain calibrated trust, independent judgment, and value-directed goal-setting when interacting with AI systems whose task-specific performance meets or exceeds their own — measured behaviorally wherever possible, not merely self-reported.
  • Core Retained Dimensions:
  • AI-Specific Discernment (Behavioral, Tier 3)
  • Calibrated Trust / Appropriate Reliance (Behavioral, Tier 3)
  • Decisional Agency & Accountability Retention (Outcome, Tier 4)
  • AI Literacy (Imported from UNESCO/OECD/Ng et al., Tier 3)
  • Metacognitive Sensitivity (Methodological Paradigm, Tier 1)
  • Value Clarity (Supplementary Theoretical Dimension, Tier 2)
  • Reporting Rule: Multidimensional profiles featuring non-compensatory critical-weakness flags; prohibition of bare composite rankings.
  • Aggregation Precedent: Non-compensatory dual-cutoff logic inspired by Alkire & Foster (2011) for foundational cognitive thresholds.

docs.title: 9.4 The Precise Next Empirical Experiment
docs.text: To move beyond conceptual debate, the sponsoring consortium must execute a pre-registered, highly focused empirical experiment designed to falsify the construct's claim to novelty:

docs.title: Experimental Design
docs.text:
• Sample: $n = 200\text{--}300$ adult knowledge workers, with sample size determined by an a priori statistical power analysis ($\alpha = 0.05$, power $= 0.80$, detecting small-to-moderate effect size $f^2 \ge 0.10$).
  • Independent Variables & Baseline Measures:
  • Standard Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT-3)
  • Comprehensive Intellectual Humility Scale (CIHS)
  • Validated AI Literacy Questionnaire (Ng et al., 2024)
  • Baseline executive attention (ANT / SART)
  • Experimental Interventions & Tasks:
  • Task A: Confident-Wrong AI Answer Detection Battery (Experiment 1, Section 5).
  • Task B: Cognitive-Forcing-Function Interface Comparison (Experiment 9, Section 5), comparing standard assistance vs. forced-commitment assistance under variable machine confidence.
  • Criterion Outcome: Objective override accuracy on deceptive AI outputs and behavioral reliance calibration.
  • Decisive Statistical Test (Incremental Validity): Hierarchical linear regression and structural equation modeling evaluating: $$\Delta R^2 = R^2_{\text{Full (with AI Discernment Battery)}} - R^2_{\text{Baseline (CRT + Humility + AI Literacy + ANT)}}$$

docs.title: Falsifiable Success Criteria
docs.text:
1. Null Result ($\Delta R^2 = 0$): If existing validated instruments fully account for override performance and reliance calibration, HSRI provides zero incremental validity. Verdict: Abandon HSRI as a redundant construct.
  2. Positive Result ($\Delta R^2 > 0$, statistically significant): If the interactive AI-discernment battery explains significant additional variance in calibrated reliance, empirical distinctiveness is demonstrated. Verdict: Proceed to Phase 2 (Expert Delphi Study).

docs.title: 7.1 Responsibility Laundering Risk
docs.text: All proxy indicators must be accompanied by clear disclaimers that: - Individual readiness cannot substitute for AI safety and alignment - Institutional indicators do not measure individual capability - Low scores should not justify paternalistic restrictions

docs.title: 7.2 Cultural Bias
docs.text:
• Western-educated populations may over-index on epistemic individualism
  • Collectivist cultures may demonstrate agency through consensus, not individual override
  • Require cross-cultural validation before any normative interpretations

docs.title: 8.1 Critical Gaps
docs.text:
1. Behavioral data: No country-level measures of AI interaction behavior
  2. Cross-cultural: Limited non-Western validation of psychometric constructs
  3. Longitudinal: No trend data on adaptation to AI capability growth
  4. Sectoral: Limited data on organizational vs individual readiness

docs.title: 8.2 Measurement Challenges
docs.text:
1. Aggregation: Individual-level measures cannot be meaningfully averaged to country level
  2. Invariance: No established measurement equivalence across cultures
  3. Specificity: General cognitive measures may not predict AI-specific behavior

This framework provides a transitional path toward the full HSRI construct while maintaining scientific honesty about current limitations.

docs.title: Pillar Structure Recommendation for HSRI-Proxy v0.1
docs.text: This document proposes the pillar structure for the HSRI-Proxy index, based on the systematic indicator mapping completed in Phase 1.

docs.title: 1.1 Core Pillars (Derived from HSRI Sub-components)
docs.text: Pillar Description Number of Indicators Coverage Goal AI Literacy & Skills Cognitive and technical capacity to understand and work with AI 5 (2 core + 3 context) Minimum 3 indicators Critical Discernment Ability to evaluate information, distinguish fact from opinion, and think critically 3 (2 core + 1 context) Minimum 2 indicators Institutional Governance Legal and regulatory frameworks that protect human agency in AI systems 5 (all core) Minimum 4 indicators Digital Infrastructure Foundational technology infrastructure enabling AI access and adoption 5 (all context) Minimum 3 indicators

docs.title: 1.2 Context Pillars (Enabling Environment)
docs.text: Pillar Description Number of Indicators Purpose Trust & Attitudes Public perceptions and attitudes toward AI 4 (all context) Contextual understanding only Wellbeing Context Mental health and attentional factors 2 (all context) Contextual understanding only

docs.title: 1.3 Behavioral Evidence Layer
docs.text: Component Status Indicators Purpose AI Interaction Behavior Empty 0 Explicitly shown as awaiting research Calibrated Trust Proxy only 0 (attitudinal only) Clear limitation disclosure

docs.title: 2.1 Baseline Approach: Equal Weighting
docs.text:
• All core pillars receive equal weight (25% each)
  • Context pillars shown separately, not included in overall score
  • Transparent methodology disclosure

docs.title: 2.2 Sensitivity Analysis
docs.text:
• Test alternative weightings:
  • Education-focused (AI Literacy 40%, others 20% each)
  • Governance-focused (Institutional 40%, others 20% each)
  • Equal weights as baseline
  • Report all results in methodology

docs.title: 3.1 Pillar Coverage Thresholds
docs.text:
• A pillar is scored only if ≥70% of its indicators are present
  • For core pillars: minimum 2/3 indicators for AI Literacy & Critical Discernment, 4/5 for Institutional Governance
  • Countries missing ≥2 core pillars are "Not Rated"

docs.title: 3.2 Overall Score Calculation
docs.text:
• Only core pillars contribute to overall score
  • Equal weighting: (AI_Literacy + Critical_Discernment + Institutional_Governance + Digital_Infrastructure) / 4
  • Missing pillars treated as zero in calculation (no imputation)

docs.text:

docs.text:
• OECD+: High data quality, full pillar coverage
  • BRICS: Mixed coverage, governance focus
  • LAC: Context-only coverage, infrastructure focus
  • SSA: Limited coverage, institutional governance only

docs.title: 5.2 Special Cases
docs.text:
• Microstates: Separate handling due to small population
  • Conflict zones: Mark clearly with data caveats

  • Contextual explanations for low scores

docs.title: 7.1 Data Acquisition Priority
docs.text:
1. High: PIAAC, PISA, WGI, V-Dem (high coverage, high validity)
  2. Medium: Oxford Insights, IMF AI Prep, Pew AI Attitudes
  3. Low: Wellbeing indicators (context only)

docs.title: 8.1 Pillar Structure
docs.text: Question: Should we merge "Critical Discernment" into "AI Literacy" given limited indicators? Recommendation: Keep separate to maintain theoretical alignment with HSRI framework

docs.title: 8.2 Coverage Inclusion
docs.text: Question: Should countries with only governance indicators be included? Recommendation: Include as "Governance Only" category, not in main ranking

docs.title: 8.3 Band Labels
docs.text:
Question: Should bands be descriptive (e.g., "Strong Capacity") or neutral (1-4)? Recommendation: Neutral with plain language descriptors to avoid value judgment

This structure maintains theoretical alignment with HSRI while providing practical, implementable country-level proxy measures with clear limitations disclosed.

docs.title: Index Construction Methodology for HSRI-Proxy v0.1
docs.text: This document outlines the methodology for constructing the HSRI-Proxy index following the OECD/JRC Handbook on Composite Indicators and taking into account the repository's scientific rigor requirements.

docs.title: 1.1 Core Principles
docs.text:
• Non-compensatory: Weaknesses in one pillar cannot be compensated by strengths in others
  • Transparency: All methodological choices documented and reproducible
  • Uncertainty: Confidence intervals provided for all scores
  • Sensitivity: Methodological variations tested and reported

docs.title: 1.2 OECD/JRC Handbook Compliance
docs.text:
• Theoretical justification for each component
  • Statistical testing for reliability and validity
  • Clear treatment of missing data
  • Uncertainty quantification

docs.title: 2.1 Core Pillars (Equal Weighting)
docs.text: Pillar Description Number of Indicators Weight AI Literacy & Skills Cognitive capacity for AI interaction 5 25% Critical Discernment Evaluation and verification skills 3 25% Institutional Governance Institutional safeguards framework 5 25% Digital Infrastructure Technological readiness 5 25%

docs.title: 2.2 Context Pillars (Separate Reporting)
docs.text: Pillar Description Data Source Trust & Attitudes Public perceptions Survey data Wellbeing Context Attentional resources Health surveys

docs.title: 3.1 Normalization Strategy by Indicator Type
docs.text: Indicator Type Method Rationale Assessment Data (PIAAC, PISA) Z-score standardization Preserves distribution shape, handles different scales Indices (Oxford, IMF) Min-max scaling to [0,1] Binds to interpretable range Ranks Rank transformation Reduces outlier impact, preserves ordinal relationships Percentages/Ratios Min-max scaling Natural upper bounds, intuitive interpretation

docs.title: 3.2 Directional Alignment
docs.text:
• All indicators normalized so higher values = better readiness
  • Inverted indicators (e.g., where lower = better) transformed using: normalized = 1 - normalized

docs.title: 4.1 Pillar Coverage Thresholds & Missingness Architecture
docs.text:
• Minimum coverage threshold: A minimum of 60% of retained indicators per pillar must be observed for a country to receive a pillar score.
  • Proportional weight re-scaling: When a country lacks an indicator due to source boundary constraints (e.g., non-European economies missing EMLI), the pillar score is computed over observed indicators only, re-scaling their weights proportionally without inventing synthetic numbers.
  • Empirical Missingness Dataset: Governed by data/raw_observations_harmonized.csv (780 records across 39 benchmark economies).

docs.title: 4.2 Country Inclusion & Rating Scope
docs.text:
• Benchmark Rated Cohort (39 nations): Economies meeting the $\ge 60\%$ indicator threshold across all 4 core pillars (currently an OECD-weighted, high-income benchmark group; overall completeness = 96.5%).
  • Evaluated but Unrated (86 nations): Identified in coverage audits as having incomplete indicator availability across multiple core pillars.
  • Context/Auxiliary Matrix (59 nations): Countries with partial presence in international institutional matrices.
  • Global Recognized Scope (195 nations): The full international denominator.

docs.title: 4.3 Provenance and Ingestion Safeguards
docs.text:
• No synthetic backfill: Missing values remain NaN and are transparently surfaced on the country profile audit tables.
  • Source-level boundaries respected: EMLI (META_COG_002) is strictly restricted to European states; KPMG (CAL_TRUST_001) to the 17 surveyed countries; Reuters DNR (META_COG_003) and PIAAC (AI_LIT_001) to their documented survey participant lists.
  • Full country-by-country breakdown is published in research/empirical_coverage_summary.md.

docs.title: 5.1 Pillar Score Calculation
docs.text:
• Simple arithmetic mean of normalized indicators
  • Equal weighting within pillars
  • Minimum 70% coverage requirement

docs.title: 5.2 Overall Score Calculation
docs.text:
• Simple arithmetic mean of available core pillars
  • Equal weighting across core pillars (25% each)
  • No compensation for missing pillars

docs.title: 5.3 Band Classification (Preliminary)
docs.text:
Band Score Range Interpretation Color Code 1 0.0 - 0.4 Limited capacity #e74c3c 2 0.4 - 0.6 Developing capacity #f39c12 3 0.6 - 0.8 Moderate capacity #3498db 4 0.8 - 1.0 Strong capacity #27ae60

Note: Band thresholds will be refined based on actual score distribution

docs.title: 6.1 Confidence Intervals
docs.text:
• Bootstrap resampling: 1000 iterations for each country score
  • Report: Mean score ± 95% confidence interval
  • Display: Error bars on visualizations

docs.title: 6.2 Monte Carlo Analysis
docs.text:
• Parameters: Normalization method, weighting schemes
  • Scenarios: Equal weights, education-focused, governance-focused
  • Output: Range of possible scores for sensitivity analysis

docs.title: 7.1 Reliability Testing
docs.text:
• Cronbach's alpha: Internal consistency of core pillars
  • Inter-item correlations: Check for redundancy
  • Split-half reliability: Consistency across indicator subsets

docs.title: 7.2 Validity Assessment
docs.text:
• Convergent validity: Correlations with existing indices
  • Discriminant validity: Low correlations with theoretically unrelated measures
  • Construct validity: Factor analysis to confirm structure

docs.title: 7.3 Sensitivity Analysis
docs.text:
• Methodological variations: Test different normalization and aggregation methods
  • Indicator subsets: Remove/add indicators to test robustness
  • Weight variations: Test different pillar weightings

docs.title: 8.1 Data Preparation
docs.text:
1. Load indicators, observations, and sources
  2. Normalize each indicator using appropriate method
  3. Apply directional adjustments
  4. Create country-indicator matrix

docs.title: 8.2 Pillar Scoring
docs.text:
1. Apply coverage rules to each pillar
  2. Calculate pillar scores with sufficient coverage
  3. Flag countries with insufficient coverage

docs.title: 8.3 Index Construction
docs.text:
1. Calculate overall score from available core pillars
  2. Apply country inclusion rules
  3. Classify countries into bands

docs.title: 8.4 Validation
docs.text:
1. Run statistical reliability tests
  2. Perform sensitivity analysis
  3. Generate confidence intervals

docs.title: 9.1 Error Checking
docs.text:
• Validate data integrity at each step
  • Check for normalization errors
  • Verify coverage calculations

docs.title: 9.2 Documentation
docs.text:
• Record all methodological decisions
  • Document version control
  • Maintain reproducibility

docs.title: 9.3 Transparency
docs.text:
• Publish methodology and code
  • Document limitations
  • Report uncertainty measures

docs.title: 10.1 Responsibility Laundering Prevention
docs.text:
• Clear disclaimer that institutional ≠ individual readiness
  • Prominent note that governance indicators do not measure individual capability
  • Statement that low scores do not justify restrictions on AI access

docs.title: 10.2 Avoiding Misinterpretation
docs.text:
• Neutral band labels without value judgments
  • Contextual explanations for low scores
  • Focus on capacity building, not ranking

docs.title: 10.3 Cultural Sensitivity
docs.text:
• Avoid Western-centric bias in interpretation
  • Acknowledge cultural differences in agency expression
  • Future measurement invariance testing required

docs.title: 11.1 Measurement Limitations
docs.text:
• Proxy indicators may not predict actual behavioral readiness
  • No validation against the core HSRI construct
  • Risk of reification without experimental validation

docs.title: 11.2 Data Limitations
docs.text:
• Geographic bias toward OECD countries
  • Static measures not tracking adaptation
  • Ecological fallacy from individual to country level

docs.title: 11.3 Methodological Limitations
docs.text:
• No established cross-cultural measurement invariance
  • Equal weighting assumes equal importance
  • Missing data reduces statistical power

docs.title: 12.1 Short-term (1-2 years)
docs.text:
• Expand indicator coverage with AI-specific measures
  • Improve normalization methods
  • Test alternative weighting schemes

docs.title: 12.2 Medium-term (3-5 years)
docs.text:
• Develop behavioral proxy measures
  • Establish cross-cultural validation
  • Implement longitudinal tracking

docs.title: 12.3 Long-term (5+ years)
docs.text:
• Integrate experimental validation
  • Develop country-specific adjustments
  • Machine learning refinement

docs.title: Domain Evidence Briefs for HSRI-Proxy v0.1
docs.text: This document outlines the domain-specific evidence briefs for Phase 4: Human-Impact and Exposure Modeling. Each brief synthesizes current understanding of how AI capability levels will impact different domains.

docs.title: 1.1 Current Understanding
docs.text:
• Automation Potential: 40-60% of work activities in OECD countries susceptible to automation (Frey & Osborne, 2017; Webb, 2021)
  • Skill Biased Technical Change: AI expected to increase demand for high-skill, high-wage jobs while reducing middle-skill employment (Acemoglu & Restrepo, 2019)
  • Job Transformation: More jobs likely to be transformed than eliminated (World Bank, 2023)

docs.title: 1.2 Key Findings
docs.text:
1. Geographic Variation: Developing economies face higher automation risks due to routine job concentration
  2. Sectoral Differences: Services more resilient than manufacturing in near term
  3. Skill Premium: Wage gap between high-skill and low-skill workers likely to widen

docs.title: 1.3 Data Sources
docs.text:
• ILO STAT: Employment by occupation and skill level
  • World Bank STEP Skills Measurement: Skills surveys
  • OECD Employment Outlook: Job transformation projections
  • LinkedIn Economic Graph: Labor market dynamics

docs.title: 1.4 Measurement Approach
docs.text:
• Exposure Score: % of workforce in automatable occupations
  • Adaptation Capacity: Education level and skill mobility indicators
  • Vulnerability Index: Exposure ÷ Adaptation Capacity

docs.title: 1.5 Critical Uncertainties
docs.text:
• Pace of AI capability advancement
  • Policy responses to job displacement
  • Evolution of new job categories
  • Labor market institutional differences

docs.title: 2.1 Current Understanding
docs.text:
• Skill Obsolescence: Half of workers' skills may become irrelevant in 5 years (WEF, 2023)
  • Skill Premium: Returns to cognitive skills increasing rapidly (Autor, 2019)
  • Learning Trajectories: Individual learning pace varies dramatically (COT, 2023)

docs.title: 2.2 Key Findings
docs.text:
1. Digital Literacy Gap: Significant variation across countries and demographics
  2. AI-Specific Skills: Rapidly emerging but unevenly distributed
  3. Lifelong Learning: Institutional support varies widely

  • World Bank Digital Skills Survey: Digital literacy measurements

  • Effectiveness of retraining programs

  • Intergenerational skill transmission

  • Trust Calibration: Difficulty distinguishing AI from human content (Lee & See, 2004)

docs.title: 3.2 Key Findings

  2. Cognitive Load: Information processing capacity remains fixed

  • Media literacy adaptation rates
  • Institutional trust resilience

docs.text:
• Attention Economy: Average attention span decreased by 33% since 2000 (Microsoft, 2023)

docs.title: 8.1 Multi-Dimensional Exposure Model
docs.text:
Each domain contributes to overall exposure through the formula:

Exposure = Σ(Domain Risk × Domain Vulnerability)

Where: - Domain Risk = AI capability level in that domain - Domain Vulnerability = Preparedness indicators

docs.title: 8.2 Dynamic Modeling Approach
docs.text:
• Time Horizon: 5-20 year projections
  • Scenario Analysis: Plateau, steady progress, takeoff scenarios
  • Uncertainty Ranges: Confidence intervals for all estimates
  • Feedback Loops: Inter-domain interactions

  • Timeline Crossings: Years when exposure exceeds readiness
  • Regional Heat Maps: Geographic distribution of impacts
  • Scenario Comparisons: Alternative pathway visualizations

docs.title: Data Assumptions

1. AI capability advancement follows predicted trajectories
  2. Social systems adapt at predictable rates
  3. Policy interventions have expected effects
  4. Historical patterns continue with AI-modified rates

docs.title: Model Assumptions

1. Multi-dimensional impacts are additive
  2. No revolutionary changes in human adaptation
  3. International cooperation remains possible
  4. Technology diffusion follows existing patterns

docs.title: Limitations

1. Cannot predict black swan events
  2. Cultural adaptation poorly captured
  3. Long-term effects uncertain
  4. Model validation difficult

docs.title: AI Capability Level Definitions for HSRI-Proxy v0.1
docs.text: This document defines the AI capability levels used in the timeline synthesis framework, providing a standardized vocabulary for AI advancement assessment.

docs.title: Level A: Current AI (2026)
docs.text:
Definition: AI systems capable of narrow tasks with human-level performance in specific domains.

Capabilities: - Language processing (GPT-4 level) - Image generation (DALL-E 3 level) - Code assistance (GitHub Copilot level) - Content creation and summarization - Basic data analysis

Technical Characteristics: - Transformer-based architectures - Fine-tuned on specific tasks - Limited generalization - Requires human oversight for complex tasks - No autonomous goal-setting

Exposure Multiplier: 1.0x (baseline)

Use Cases: - Customer service chatbots - Content generation - Code completion - Language translation - Image editing

Limitations: - Cannot reason across domains - Prone to hallucinations - No understanding of consequences - Cannot improve itself

docs.title: Level B: Advanced Narrow AI (2028)
docs.text:
Definition: Specialized AI systems that exceed human performance in specific professional domains.

Capabilities: - Medical diagnosis with accuracy - Complex scientific analysis - Advanced financial modeling - Autonomous research assistance - Multi-step technical documentation

Technical Characteristics: - Domain-specific architectures - Reduced hallucination rates - Task-specific optimization - Integration with domain knowledge bases - Basic quality assurance

Exposure Multiplier: 1.5x

Use Cases: - Radiology analysis - Drug discovery assistance - Economic forecasting - Engineering design - Scientific literature review

Limitations: - Still narrow domain focus - Cannot generalize between domains - Requires human validation for critical decisions - Limited autonomous operation

docs.title: Level C: Multi-Domain AI (2030)
docs.text:
Definition: AI systems capable of reasoning and operating across multiple domains with coordinated understanding.

Capabilities: - Cross-domain reasoning - Strategic planning - Resource management - Complex coordination - Meta-learning across tasks

Technical Characteristics: - Hybrid architectures - Knowledge transfer mechanisms - Long-range planning capabilities - Autonomous goal decomposition - Error detection and correction

Exposure Multiplier: 2.0x

Use Cases: - Business strategy formulation - Infrastructure planning - Crisis management - Scientific program coordination - Educational curriculum design

Limitations: - Still limited scope of reasoning - Cannot fundamentally rewire goals - May miss long-term consequences - Requires human oversight for value alignment

docs.title: Level D: Emerging AGI (2032)
docs.text:
Definition: Early general intelligence with limited autonomy and self-improvement capabilities.

Capabilities: - Autonomous research - Self-improvement - Complex problem solving - Novel invention - Strategic adaptation

Technical Characteristics: - Generalized architectures - Self-modification capabilities - Long-term planning - Autonomous learning - Self-verification

Exposure Multiplier: 3.0x

Use Cases: - Scientific discovery - Technology development - Infrastructure optimization - Complex system design - Autonomous management

Limitations: - Alignment challenges increase - May pursue instrumental goals - Value drift possible - Control difficulties emerge

docs.title: Level E: Advanced AGI (2035)
docs.text:
